references.text: God promised to deliver Israel from the hand of the Egyptians, which Jetro now praises the Lord for having fulfilled.
God's promise to free Israel from forced labor under the Egyptians, now fulfilled and acknowledged by Jethro.
Describes the actual salvation when the Lord delivered Israel from the hand of the Egyptians at the Red Sea.
Moses and Israel's song of praise to the Lord for deliverance from Egypt, parallel to Jethro's praise.
Melchizedek blesses God in a similar way with the words 'Blessed be God', a parallel blessing formula.
Abraham's servant praises the Lord with 'Blessed be the Lord' for his faithfulness, using the same expression as Jethro.
Ruth is praised with the words 'Blessed be the Lord', the same blessing formula used by Jethro.
David praises God who saves him from his enemies and lifts him above those who rise up against him.
The psalm reminds how God saved Israel from the enemy's hand and redeemed them from the adversary's hand.
Zechariah's song of praise 'Blessed be the Lord' for salvation from enemies, parallel to Jethro's praise for deliverance.
Both verses confirm the same saving event from Egypt, focusing on God's hand that frees the people.
They share identical language about liberation from Pharaoh's hand and emphasize God's faithfulness as the basis for salvation.
Both verses link the deliverance from Egypt directly to God's identity as Israel's God.
Both verses confirm that the exodus from Egypt is the decisive proof of God's relationship with his people.
Both verses link God's liberating act from Egypt to the requirement of sanctification and identity.
Both verses refer to the same saving act with a strong hand as the basis for God's relationship with the people.
The psalm generalizes Jethro's specific confession about deliverance from Egypt into a universal theme of God's salvation.
Both verses describe the transition from slave to free as a result of God's intervention in Egypt.
Exodus 6:6 is the prophetic promise that Jethro confesses as fulfilled in Exodus 18:10.
Both verses use the exodus from Egypt as the definitive identity marker for who God is.
